utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. May I remind you of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence which still applies. We will continue now with the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom; good afternoon, Witness. We are today the 8th of March, and let me avail myself of this opportunity to wish everyone Happy International Women's Day. Let us pick up where we left off, and those were the events of the hospital. I will ask you a couple of more questions concerning the hospital. Let me remind you of the need to make a brief pause before the answer for the sake of the interpreters, not for my sake, so that the record may be a true reflection of what we are saying. I'd ask you during your stay at the Vukovar hospital, did you see Vesna Bosanac? Do you know who she is?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me how many times?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how many times I saw her, but I used to see her at the hospital. She was the administrator, wasn't she.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe you saw her at the MUP as well. Did she used to come there?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw her at the hospital, not the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the MUP.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see her at the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know perhaps anyone else from among the staff of the hospital? Did you get to know anyone?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got to know a lot of them, but I don't remember their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Dr. Njavro?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I saw him but I didn't get to know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: How have Binazija Kolesar?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I said no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of Marin Vidic, Bili?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have heard of him. I even think he was at the military investigations prison in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge, direct or otherwise, that he was at the hospital at the time when you were there?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many people at the hospital. I really don't know all their names. Whether Vidic, Bili was there or not I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Let me take you back to the part of your testimony related to your stay at the MUP or your tenure at the MUP. You said you don't know whether Vesna Bosanac had ever come to the MUP for an interview or anything. Do you know that anyone else from the hospital came to the police station while Stipe Pole was the chief for an interview, a discussion, or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You described yesterday your position and the position of your colleague Mr. Zlogledja, and in response to Mr. Borovic's questions you said there were about 100 members of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say a hundred.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, tell me how many then.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. What do these figures have to do with anything? How many civilians, how many policemen. What does all that have to do with Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you are here to answer my questions. I am questioning you, not the other way around, and it is up to the Trial Chamber to decide whether something is relevant or not, and if it isn't relevant they will stop my questioning.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot give you a number. Maybe there were more than a hundred, maybe less than a hundred.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I can live with that answer as well. Can you tell us this: Where and at which positions the other members of the MUP were deployed while you were occupying the position of Sunce facing the Danube and your colleague Zlogledja facing Luzac?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where they were deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: After this break-through which you call a failed attempt to leave Vukovar, do you know what happened to those members of the MUP? Did they stay in Vukovar or did they manage to get out?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you some of them managed to get out. Others stayed behind. I told you yesterday that Zlatko, Kuscevic, Hrkic, and I went back to the hospital. What happened with the rest, I don't know whether they managed to break through or not. I don't know. Some of them came back to the hospital as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many of them in addition to the four of you, more than a hundred or less than a hundred, returned to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there were some other groups of people who were involved in what you call the defence of Vukovar who tried to get out of Vukovar did not succeed and returned to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no such information. Maybe, maybe no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You said Zlogledja yourself discarded your weapons at the cemetery?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me how far that is from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. In terms of metres or kilometres, I have no idea. I know it was dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the others who returned together with you, members of the MUP or others did with their weapons?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. They must have thrown it away, just like I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose some of them were in uniform.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible too. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you to tell me only about the things you know. If you don't know something, that's no problem. Do you know that some of them entered the hospital in uniform?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I doubt it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, on the 20th in the morning when you left the hospital, among the people who were outside the hospital who were being inspected by the troops, by the army in the way you described, did you see any of the MUP members whom you knew wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Next to me there was a man from Varazdin wearing the uniform trousers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You now mention this Varazdin man and you answered my colleague's question about the involvement of policemen from Varazdin?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And at one point you said that many from the territory of the entire Croatia defended Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they must have. They were from Varazdin after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from those policemen from Varazdin, from which other towns in Croatia were there policemen who were involved in the defence of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I only know about the man from Varazdin.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: We have a -- we need to clarify something. So you don't know from what other towns or areas people came to defend Vukovar except those men from Varazdin?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have no such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the fact that in addition to those men from Varazdin, Croats, some foreigners also fought on the side of the Croatian state, of the Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I really don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear while you were at the hospital that there were some foreign nationals at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You did not hear about that?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You say that after that you were taken away. We discussed yesterday the time you spent outside the hangar. You described the spot where the four of you stood. What I want to know is this: While you were standing there, this indefinite amount of time which you said was an hour, two hours, or maybe more or less, it doesn't matter, did you see that apart from you standing there there was another group of people standing elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you there were some children standing outside the door of the hangar, four or five children. I know some children had been there. What became of them, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you possibly see an officer of the Yugoslav People's Army entering the hangar, taking somebody out, and leaving that person standing outside?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that. I saw an officer come up to the door, look in and close the door back.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I'm now talking about Ovcara, the hangar at Ovcara, and I'm asking you about officers. Now I'm asking you about any member of the armed units present there. Did any member of armed units present there take anyone out of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: They transferred you in the way you described to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You said you spent three days there.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In some basement?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how many of there were you in that room?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from the four of us, I think there were about 20 civilians and one wounded person from Varazdin on a stretcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, tell me, were you able during the night to talk amongst yourselves?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: While the active-duty soldiers were inside, yes, we talked. Not to the civilians though.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: But amongst yourselves?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, amongst ourselves. Yes, we did talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: During the whole time, was there at all times a member of the Yugoslav People's Army together with you inside?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All the time?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the evening they would play music to those people, civilians. They would dance with them, hit them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You told us about that. Have you heard about a man called Sinisa Glavasevic?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know he was a journalist. I know -- in fact, I think he was taken out of the Vukovar Hospital. I didn't know him really, but I heard of him. He was an anchor at Radio Vukovar, a presenter. He had a Band-Aid on his eye, and when he was leaving the hospital he turned back and made a gesture to say hello, but a soldier hit him in the back with a rifle-butt. Later I didn't see him anymore. I didn't see him at the basement either.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: That's precisely what I want to ask you. That man whom you heard was Sinisa Glavasevic, did you see him at Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I can't say I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: There is a little point in the transcript that we need to clarify. What did you say Sinisa Glavasevic was taken out the hospital?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning of the 20th, like we were. I didn't know him personally but somebody told me it was Sinisa Glavasevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dodaj, I'm going to ask you some things that we need to clarify from the personal details you provided in all of your statements. I see that you are retired.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you from 1991 onwards, from the point you were released from prison in Valjevo, what have you been doing?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: After.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I did?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What did you do for a living?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not do any manual work because the doctor told me I should not lift more than five kilos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't understand me. I'm not asking about that. What was your occupation? What did you do? Were you employed anywhere?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, then, how you came to be retired?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I was a member of the 204th Brigade. I had been released from a camp, a prison, and that's how I got the status of a retiree.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Are you drawing an allowance, a disability or other allowance or an indemnification on account of the time you spent in prison?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indemnification?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: And who would be giving me that indemnification?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't them who beat me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. I'd like to ask you something.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that I got a higher rank from them and that's why my pension is higher than it would have been?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: A rank?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The rank is the equivalent of what in the JNA would have been staff sergeant.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I understand, the time you spent there counted towards your career in the army or the time you spent fighting as a soldier?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you stay in touch with any of the people with whom you had spent this entire time in prison and then in the camp?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have stayed in touch with Zlatko only.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Are you in touch frequently?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We speak on the phone about two or three times a year, but we have not yet managed to visit each other. I hope to go and see him soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the last time you met Zlatko Zlogledja?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was back in 1998 here in The Hague. As for the last time I spoke to him on the phone, I think it was just before Christmas. I called to say Merry Christmas.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Back in 1998 when you met here, were you staying at the same hotel?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: How many times did you spend together here?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It's difficult to say. Perhaps about a week or less. I can't say. About a week, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see him every evening, every day?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We saw a lot of each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Zlatko Zlogledja testified before the court in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't. He is a mentally destroyed man, a broken man.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When you say devastated or "mentally destroyed," what exactly do you mean when you say that?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: He has trouble sleeping. His legs keep swelling, and he has trouble with his spinal column too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You live near Bjelovar?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: How many inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At last local elections I think the count was about 520. That's about as much as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a brief comment. In relation to the -- the specific details of where the witness lives, despite the fact that he's not a protected witness, I just wonder whether they could be redacted from the transcript. I'm not sure whether it's completely necessary that the specifics of his address are made public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That would appear not to be of any problem to you, would it, Mr. Bulatovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, no problem at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, we will redact it looks like line 25 of 10 and 1 and 2 of 11 would probably do the job, would it, Mr. Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dodaj, during your testimony in chief or in cross-examination, you said a particular sentence. You said that back in 1991, you weren't interested in politics at all. What I want to know is: Did you get involved in politics at any point in time after 1991?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I am the president of the HSP branch in my own village.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please explain the Court what the HSP party is?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the Croatian party of rights. If I may just be allowed to add something.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask my question and you can add whatever you like. Throughout the fighting in Vukovar back in 1991, the HSP, did the party have any armed units of its own?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. What I wanted to tell you is when I became a member. That was later on. It was during the local elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Which year was that?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: 2004, I think. 2003 possibly. I'm not sure when the local elections took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Who is the president of that party?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my village, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: No. The party president, the top man.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ante Djapic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: He is now the mayor of Osijek, right?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that party preserved the traditions of the party from which it was originally created?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who the founding father of the party was back then, as it were?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that at the outset there was Paraga. There was someone else back in 1860-something.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to that, I'm in possession of certain information and you can confirm that or deny that, you were one of the leaders of your party at the local level.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did tell you that I'm the party president of that particular local branch. But, Your Honours, I'm really unsure about what that has to do with my testimony here, my membership in the party or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dodaj, the same applies as before. Should I ask any questions that are not allowed, the OTP are likely to react and stop that from happening, as is the Trial Chamber. I'm about to ask you some other questions, but again it's about your political involvement. And I'm nearing the end of my cross-examination as well. Are you a member of the local board for self-government in Bjelovar municipality?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us more about that?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I didn't make the list or, actually, you could say that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Are you the president of the board for sports and culture in Severin municipality?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as well as president of the local football club in my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of Ante Pavelic?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was told back at school that he was a war criminal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: A war criminal.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was or not, but that's history, isn't it? Am I being tested here or is this a history lesson?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: No, but I'd like to ask you something else. Do you know that Ante Pavelic first founded your party. Dobroslav Paraga then continued his work and after them came Ante Djapic. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know about that, but I can tell you about my own involvement. I got support for my membership by a lot of the local Serbs. I am president of the football club, and there are many Serb -- Serbian lads involved in the football club. I get on with them just fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the statute or platform of your political party?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I'm not interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And it's pointless for me to indicate to you that according to your party statute only Croats can become members, I suppose? Your Honours, this concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is just not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Just a few questions in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, you said that when you were released from prison that you were given the status of a member of the 204th Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And was that for your service, the time that you spent in Vukovar for those two months that you were on guard duty?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The two months that I spent in Vukovar, plus the time I spent in detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you were in Vukovar in 1991, did you know whether the 204th Brigade existed at that time?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I'd just like to ask you a couple of questions about your knowledge of the defence of Vukovar. In response to my learned friend's questions on whether or not certain parts of Vukovar were defended, you said in relation to Bogdanovci, Luzac, Mitnica, Borovo, and the fair-grounds that they were probably defended. Do you remember saying something to that effect?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have said something to that effect, possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And just to understand your knowledge of the extent of the defence of those areas, in relation to Bogdanovci, do you know how many men defended that area?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know in relation to Bogdanovci or other parts of Vukovar. I can't give you a figure. It wasn't much of a resistance in terms of what the military had. Had the army wanted to break into Vukovar much sooner, I believe they could have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And I would like to show you your 1994 statement that you gave to the Croatian authorities now. The B/C/S copy will be passed to you. Do you have the copy of that statement that you gave the Croatian authorities in 1994 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, in cross-examination it's been put to you that there was a couple of matters that have been left out of that statement but have been mentioned in your testimony over the last couple of days. I would just like to ask you how many pages does that statement contain?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if you look at the top right-hand corner of that statement, do you agree with me that the statement or the note was made on the 11th of February, 1994?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if you look further down, do you agree with me that you gave this information to the police on the 1st of February, 1994, some ten days earlier?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you look at the last page of that Official Note, and can you tell me whose signature appears at the end?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't. What it says is Drazen Divic [phoen]. I'm not sure if he is the one who signed this. Sir, I was questioned on Bjelovar for two days from 7.00 a.m. to 3.00 p.m., and I don't think they could possibly have fitted the entire thing into these four or five sheets of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And does your signature appear on that statement at all?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can't see my signature anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And after you gave -- after you gave that statement, was the Official Note ever read back to you? Were you called back to the police station to read what was -- what they recorded?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If you can look at page 4 of that statement. Perhaps page 4 in the B/C/S, paragraph 5. And if you can read down, not out loud, but just look at that to paragraph -- to page 5, paragraph 1. And do you agree with me that there's about 20 lines of information that contains your experiences in Vukovar from the 19th of November till the time that you were taken to Topcider in -- near Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it seems.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Smith. You'll be pleased to know, Mr. Dodaj, that the evidence that you were asked to give is now at an end, so that you are now free to leave and go back to your home and your affairs. The Chamber would like to thank you for coming to The Hague and for the assistance that you've been able to give to us. You are now able to leave with the court officer who will show you out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The next witness is a protected witness with voice distortion. That may mean that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It does mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: It does. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We must break now to enable the voice distortion system to be set up and tested. That would normally take 15 to 20 minutes. I'm looking at the time, conscious that there was a redaction in that last programme which would require a half-hour break to enable the tapes to be dealt with. I think, looking ahead, the most practical course would be to call this now the first break of the afternoon. It might mean that at the end of the day we finish a little bit early as the tapes run out, but I don't think we need an additional break in the course of the afternoon. So we will adjourn now and resume at 25 minutes past 3.00 and have one further break after that at about an hour and 35 minutes after we resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Would you please take the card that's given to you and read aloud the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Smith has some questions for you. Yes, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, as you understand, you're a protected witness before the Tribunal. Your name and your image will not be publicised. Also, your voice is to be distorted. Because of that, we need to have a good break between the question and answer, so we'll go at a reasonably moderate pace. Witness, I'm going to produce to you now a document, and this contains your name, date of birth, and your place of birth, and can you tell the Court whether or not those details are correct.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: It's all correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I seek to tender that document under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document will be tendered -- will be admitted under seal under the reference 239.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Smith. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, you were born and raised in Vukovar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you graduated as an economist?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Yes, senior economist.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And then at the age of about 22 you got your first job in Vukovar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when did you complete or when did you undertake your national service with the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And for about how long did you do your national service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Around ten and a half months.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court what your training was -- was in in the national service, what your speciality was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Engineering training with pioneer vocation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And specifically what types of activities does that involve in layman's terms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Well, that implies putting up all sorts of obstacles in combat, especially laying mines.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And after you finished your national service, what did you do after that in terms of employment? Just generally.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I found a job for a short while at the Borovo shoe factory and later the forwarding company of Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in 1991, did you still hold that position in that company?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Yes. That was the company where I had a permanent job.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And was that company in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: The head office was in Rijeka, but the branch was in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if we talk about the beginning of 1991, say in January, what was life like in Vukovar? What were the relations like between the ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I would say that life took its normal everyday course, but some changes began to occur already, and you could not avoid politics in everyday life.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you describe to the Court what types of changes that you noticed in the beginning of 1991 from the political point of view?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Well, the first change we felt was the change in the state. The Croatian state became established, and as a result of that people started taking sides, and that's where the rift occurred. Some people were in favour of keeping the state that used to be and others favoured the newly established state, and that had its echoes in all layers of society. And all the media got involved, the television, the press, and everything else, all the mass media.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And are you able to say which ethnic groups or which people were supporting the Croatian state and which groups were supporting the former Yugoslavia state?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Well, the state of Yugoslavia was supported by the remnants of the still-active Communist Party in that area, and new parties came into being after the establishment of the new state, primarily the HDZ, the Croatian Democratic Union. They were in favour of separating from the old Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you explained, politically speaking, what changes were occurring in Vukovar. What about socially speaking? Were -- how were the ethnic groups mixing as a result of these changes occurring?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Well, I think that happened, but I didn't belong to any particular group, so it's difficult for me to elaborate on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what about in terms of violence? In 1991, when was the first time that you became aware of violence in Vukovar or in or around Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Well, some things started to happen that were out of the ordinary, bombings, explosions. Some kiosks were blown up. Clashes began in Borovo settlement and Borovo village. And these events increasingly became the focus of public attention, not only in Yugoslavia, perhaps internationally as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you talked about clashes in Borovo settlement and Borovo village. Who were the clashes between?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I can't make a judgement, but from what I know it was a clash between the legal forces of the Ministry of the Interior and the opposite side or, how shall I put it, some hostile forces from inside Borovo Selo. I can't say who it was exactly who first attacked a policeman doing their duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you talk about hostile forces from inside Borovo Selo, do you know what ethnic group those hostile forces belonged to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Well, I can only assume that those were Serbs who did not want to recognise or accept the Croatian state.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how did -- how were you able to make that assumption? Where were you getting your information from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: That's the sort of thing that you could learn in the public domain, from TV, from newspapers. That's how I learned about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when did this -- when did these clashes occur at the Borovo settlement at Borovo village approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: From what I remember, it was the 2nd of May, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And do you know what the results of those clashes were, whether there were any casualties or deaths?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Yes, there were casualties. A figure of 25 was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say 25, was that 25 deaths or 25 woundings? Can you be a little more specific?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I think there were 25 dead, but I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You also mentioned that there were some bombings and explosions occurring in and around Vukovar. Do you know who was -- who was causing these bombings to occur, or these explosions to occur?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I don't know that, but I heard about it because news of that travelled very far, far enough for me to learn about it without leaving my home.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when -- when did these bombings and explosions start?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Well, we can say that it was during the summer after the incidents in Borovo village.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And during that summer did your wife and children -- did they leave Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Yes. That happened after the shelling started, of the centre of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Perhaps if we can talk about the shelling. When did that -- when did that first start, to your knowledge, and do you know who was doing the shelling at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: From what I remember, the shelling began on the 7th of July that year, 1991, but who was responsible I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you said the centre of Vukovar was being shelled. Do you know more specifically what places in the centre of town were being shelled at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I remember some. For instance, close to Hadisa in the street that was all the Borisa Kidrica then, or the place that was a square next to a school building. There was a cross called the Becar cross. That was the target of some shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And do you know the reason why those locations were shelled?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to answer that question. I don't know whether it was intimidation or something else. I can't answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And after the shelling you said that your wife and children left Vukovar. Where did they go and how was it organised that they leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: That was organised by the Croatian Democratic Union party. They organised the departure of my wife and children in the form of a trip to the seaside that would last until things calmed down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About how many people do you know went on this -- this form of trip to the seaside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Well from, what I saw several buses left, and it took place over a couple of days. So it was rather a large number of residents who left. I mean women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And do you know whether the residents were from all the different ethnic groups that lived in Vukovar, or was it just one particular one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: At that time, nobody really cared who was of which ethnicity. At least I didn't, so I can't comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And about -- you may have said this already, but about what date did your wife and children leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I know the exact date. The 7th August, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And why was this trip organised?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I've already mentioned that. Because of the shelling of the town and the danger that started looming over us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And as a result of the shelling of the town, did any people within the town begin to defend themselves or form some sort of defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, some volunteer units began organising themselves and teams that were to put up a local defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: As far as you're concerned, when did you finish working in your job? You said at the beginning of 1991 you were working. When did you finish working?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I think it was already August 1991. I don't think we were going to work anymore. But we still kept in touch by phone or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how long was the trip planned for for your wife and children? When were they expected to come back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: The idea was for them to stay there for about two weeks, and they were to return on the 25th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, did they return, and if they didn't, why didn't they return?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: They never returned, because on the 24th -- or, rather, the 25th in the morning, the final battle for Vukovar began. The shelling was so relentless and bad that the buses that had already set off for Vukovar at 8.00 that morning were stopped near Kutina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how far is Kutina away from Vukovar approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: A little over 200 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you said that Vukovar was shelled for the first time on -- I think you said the 7th of July. Up until the 24th to the 25th of August when you say the final battle began, what sort of activity, military activity, was occurring between that period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: As far as the shelling is concerned; the shelling started even earlier, in the beginning of July, and my wife and children left town on the 7th of August. Military activities took place throughout that time, and the conflict escalated with each new day until it turned into a full-blown war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And from your perspective, who was the conflict between?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: The conflict was between the joint forces of the JNA, including all forms of, I would say, paramilitary units that participated in the concerted action of conquering Vukovar that was aimed at crushing the entire Croatian state.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what about the other side? You talked about a local defence of Vukovar. Who was on the other side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: You mean the local defence from which side?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Just referring to your answer where you said the final battle from Vukovar -- for Vukovar began. You said the JNA and the paramilitaries had a concerted action to conquer Vukovar. Who was the battle with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Well, that's precisely what the conflict was about. They were the fighting the Home Guards Corps, the Ministry of the Interior, and all the combatants who joined in the defence of Vukovar on the side of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did you join in to the defence of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Yes, I joined Vukovar's defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And why did you join it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: It was a moral duty, and at one point it became legal duty too. The entire municipality of Vukovar was mobilised, and the clashes lasted for so long with no lull or reprieve that I decided I had to do something and contribute to the town's defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When were you aware that a -- some sort of defence of the town was being set up? When were you first aware?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I first became aware of this early that summer, but I didn't join until much later. I still expected that everything would soon be back to normal, that life would soon be back to normal, a life dignified enough for human beings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you explain in a little more detail the -- the nature of the attack of Vukovar on the 24th to the 25th of August? You said that's when the final battle commenced. What was happening in Vukovar on those couple of days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: When I say the final battle, I mean the severe shelling, firing by all possible weapons, all possible calibres, from the air, from the water, and from all the surrounding areas of Vukovar. I mean this indiscriminate shelling where the targets are not necessarily of military nature. Everything that was part of the town was fair game for shelling. This means that neither animals more people were spared, regardless of their species or occupation or gender.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, here are you talking about the 24th to the 25th, or are you talking about the whole time you were in Vukovar until you left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: The severe shelling started on the morning of the 25th, possibly the evening of the 24th, and went on and on. From that day, the town was being shelled severely on a daily basis, and it only kept intensifying, if anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what date did you leave Vukovar? What date did you leave the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I never did. I joined the town's defence instead. And I remained in Vukovar until the day the town eventually fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what date did you join the town's defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to get the time-line right after so much time, but it was sometime in mid-September. We were called to a meeting at the Vukovar municipality building. This meeting was organised by the command of the town's defence. They told us that if we so wished we could get involved in the town's defence. It was from that day on that I was involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And who told you that you could get involved? What were the individuals' names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: The commander who told us this was Branko Borkovic, also known as Mladi Jastreb. He was the deputy commander, and the commander-in-chief was Mile Dedakovic, also known as Jastreb or Stari Jastreb. Another person present was Danijel Rehak. He held a post with Vukovar's national defence office.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The transcript didn't pick up the last name. You said the other person present in addition to Dedakovic and Borkovic was who?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Danijel Rehak. He held a post with the national defence office. He used to be the secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And about how many others like you were called for the meeting that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: The way I remember, there were about 50 persons in attendance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did you have a choice to join the defence or was it compulsory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Mobilisation itself was compulsory, but still we were told that if there was anyone who did not wish to join the town's defence, no grudge would be held against them and they were still free to leave the area with no consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And on that day did you accept to join?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Yes, and I was given an assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And perhaps if you could explain that to the Court, the nature of the assignment you were given, and who gave it to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: It was the deputy commander, Branko Borkovic, who told me that I would be in charge of the miners group, the engineering aspect of their work, laying obstacles along the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And do you know whether this miners group existed before you arrived, and if it did, for about how long?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I know that it had existed, but I didn't know for how long.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say "miners group," I assume you're referring to the laying of landmines.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Yes, and infantry and anti-tank mines.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And whilst we're on the topic of, say, command structure, did the command structure of the defence of Vukovar change over time whilst you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Can you please clarify that for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did Branko Borkovic always hold the deputy commander position whilst you were in Vukovar, or did that change?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: The only change was in relation to the commander himself, Stari Jastreb. He left sometime in early October, and Branko Borkovic took over. My position or my relation to the command remained unchanged until the very end.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you took over -- you were placed in charge of the miners group. Can you tell the Court the size, how many men were in that group, and in a practical way how you went about your tasks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I had about ten men in my group, but this changed over time depending on the conditions that prevailed. Jastreb would give us orders, and we would carry out assignments wherever needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And these assignments, were they to place landmines around the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Yes, predominantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you be, say, a little more specific as to where the landmines were being laid?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Wherever there were clashes or along the roads leading into the town or any other place that the enemy might have used to approach the town. Wherever the enemy was expected to come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say "the enemy," who were you referring to there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I'm referring to all the forces around Vukovar firing at Vukovar, including the JNA, all their subordinate units and all the paramilitary units that were involved in the attack on Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: From that can we gather that landmines were placed all around the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Not all around the town. Not in the town itself but along the confrontation lines and the front lines, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how long did you do this job? How long did you have this assignment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: The assignment ceased on the 16th or the 17th, on the eve of Vukovar's fall, or better yet, when the command was disbanded, when it stopped operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you said that you placed the landmines along the confrontation lines. Did the confrontation lines change over the time that you had this assignment, over that two-month period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Yes. They shifted. Some did and some didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say "they shifted," did they shift further away from Vukovar or towards Vukovar, the centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: They shifted towards the centre of town. The circle around us was tightening.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what type of landmines were you using? Just in a general sense.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: We were using all the standard mines used by the JNA, anti-infantry and anti-tank mines of different kinds.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if you could just provide the Court with an example as to how you would lay an anti-tank mine and how would you lay an anti-infantry mine or group of mines.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: There are several ways to lay those, but under those conditions we usually just scattered them as quickly as we could. We would scatter rows of mines. Anti-tank mines, for example, about four rows of those, sometimes two, depending on what we could manage. The distance between two rows would be about one metre normally. When we laid anti-personnel mines, they would be laid in areas where the enemy was expected to approach, and that's how the entire area would be blocked.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if you can explain about how many anti-tank mines and how many anti-personnel mines would be grouped together at one location approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Depending on the area to be covered. Sometimes ten mines, sometimes 20, and sometimes 50, depending on the size of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And over that two-month period, about how many different locations did you lay landmines?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Over 50, I believe, but it's difficult to say exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did you ever lay those mines in areas where there were civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: No. Only along the confrontation line and wherever there was combat. Along the line separating us from the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did you keep a record of the locations where you laid the mines?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: By all means. I kept my own record, and I would place local commanders in charge and told them to keep such records, too, and bring them regularly to their respective command posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And whose decision would it be to decide where the mines would be laid, and how would those decisions come about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Those decisions were taken by Jastreb in cooperation with the local commanders. The order would come from Jastreb alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you said that you laid mines in about 50 different locations during that time. About how many mines in total were used in those 50 locations approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: About 1.000 mines, roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of the laying of the mines? What did you believe the commander intended?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: It wasn't for me to judge what the commander's intentions were. I was there to carry out my assignment. My thoughts on this didn't matter. What mattered was for me to carry out my assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: But what were your thoughts? What was the purpose of the mines?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: The purpose of the mines was to lay obstacles along certain lines in order to keep the enemy from breaking through our lines. The purpose was to protect the town, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You talked about the shelling of the town over this two-month period. Whilst this mine-laying activity was going on, can you tell the Court the nature of the shelling and how frequent it was of the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: The objective was to crush the defenders' resistance, and the shelling was on an enormous scale. Thousands and thousands of shells were raining down on a daily basis over a limited area. It's difficult to even describe. The purpose was to wipe any life out of the area or perhaps to wipe the entire area off the face of the earth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what parts of the town were hit by the shelling and the nature of the damage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: The centre of town itself and all those areas in Vukovar that were not under their control, all the buildings were being shelled regardless of any protection, degree of protection that they enjoyed. The same applied to the hospital, to the kindergarten, to the school. Nothing was sacred at this point. Everything was fair game, and everything was a target. The targeting was not selective. Rather, it was random and frequent as well as indiscriminate. Perhaps as many as 1.000 shells per hour were being fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you describe the nature of the damage in the centre of town? Were there parts of the centre that weren't destroyed or damaged at all? Was it light damage? Was it heavy? Can you explain further.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Every day the damage became greater and greater. I wasn't aware of a single building that was intact and that was not hit by any sort of missile, bullet or shell. Even the hospital itself, the workers' hall, which was plumb in the centre of town burnt down as well. In the area in which we were taking, in that particular environment, there was not a single building that was still standing that hadn't been hit, that hadn't burned town or been damaged in some way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you talked about the centre of town. What about the suburbs of Vukovar? Were you able to say what sort of damage was caused in the houses in the suburbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: The same sort of damage as elsewhere. Units were organised in those areas, the purpose of which was to defend the town. They weren't spared the shelling either.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the nature of your job, laying the mines, did that take you all around the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Unfortunately, it did. At least those areas that one could still move about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were you able to determine what direction the attack was coming from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: All directions. It was coming from all sides, from across the Danube and all the surrounding villages; for the most part, those villages that were predominantly Serb villages. But shelling was coming from all sides, from all around.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And are you able to say what weaponry was used to attack the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Based on what we heard, based on what we experienced every day, this was heavy shelling by tanks, by guns, by mortar shells, by rifles, machine-guns, all possible sorts of weapons including planes that were dropping bombs, some as heavy as 250 kilogrammes. There were cluster bombs being dropped too. All the weapons that were available to the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know how often the planes were dropping bombs over Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I'm not sure how often, but the planes were flying overhead all the time, and it's difficult to say how frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how were people living in that two months whilst Vukovar was under attack? How were the residents living?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: The conditions were appalling. The electrician at this supply had been cut off as well as the water supply and our food. Everything was very difficult. The only way to organise ourselves was to assemble at collection centres or in cellars, and that's what most of the residents did. Even so, the suffering of everyone there was beyond words, especially if you bear in mind what the elderly and the children had to go through.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And during that two-month period, are you able to say whether all of the ethnic groups that previously lived in the town of Vukovar were still there or was there a predominance of one over the other?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Your question is somewhat difficult to understand. Can you please repeat that for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The town of Vukovar before the war, what was the ethnic composition approximately of, say, Serbs, Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I don't really know, because I never researched that particularly, but there were Croats and Serbs. And as far as I know, there were actually 23 different ethnic groups in Vukovar, but it was not my life's work to investigate who belonged where.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the question is: Did that stay the same, that mixture, during the time that Vukovar was being shelled between that two -- over that two-month period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: It stayed the same more or less because, unfortunately, both Serbs and Croats got killed and suffered a lot, although many people left and joined the attack on Vukovar, especially those who left to third places, but that's not something I can tell you much about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And from your role in the defence of Vukovar, are you able to say what the size of the defence was? About how many men were involved in the defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: That, too, is a difficult question, but from my perspective, as someone who has seen a lot, there were certainly at least a thousand people involved in the organisation of the defence, but that's my estimate. Maybe you can get confirmation from somebody else who had better insight.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And from your observations around the town, about -- what type of weaponry did the defence of the town have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: The defence of the town of relatively few weapons, mostly infantry weapons and two or three tanks that we captured during the fighting. The rest were a few mortars or two or three cannons, and all the rest were sidearms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And from your observations of the weaponry of the JNA and paramilitaries that were attacking the town compared to the amount of weaponry that the defence had, what would their -- can you give a relatively proportion between the two sides?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Well, it takes a military analyst to answer that question, but judging by the number of shells that hit us and the damage done to the town, the ratio was 1 to 100 maybe, or maybe even worse for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Where were the headquarters of the territorial -- sorry, where were the headquarters of the Croatian defence.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: The same place as before the war. Where the military department used to be. And the command was in the nuclear shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the nuclear shelter, did that have a particular name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I don't know. It's the nuclear shelter of the military department. I don't know if it had a name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And about how far away was that from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: About a kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Is that closer towards town or further away from the centre of the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: It was a kilometre away from both, but the -- the hospital was further away from the military department. In fact, it depends on where you're looking from. Could you maybe rephrase the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I think that's fine for the moment. Perhaps if we can move to the fall of Vukovar. When -- when do you say that Vukovar fell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Well, in my mind the Vukovar -- Vukovar fell when the command ceased to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court when that was and how you found out that the command ceased?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: That night of the 16th, we were involved in a mission, carrying out an assignment, and we suffered losses, both dead and wounded, and upon coming to the headquarters that day, to the command, I found it was empty. There were no commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And once you discovered that, what did you decide to do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I returned to my men, to my fellow fighters. I explained to them what had happened. I said the commanders had left their positions, and in a way informally demobed them, saying that they were free to do as they saw fit. If they wanted to, they could try to break through enemy lines and escape. I said that I personally had no where to go because my parents were still in Vukovar, and at that moment I was not prepared to leave the town yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And during this time when you were with the defence, where were you staying? Where were you sleeping at night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: We had our command position, command post, in the former building of the school for on-the-job training in the basement of that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And after you demobilised the men in your unit, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I think Mr. Lukic has got something to say, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have a small correction to the transcript. Page 38, line 18. When the witness was explaining that he told his group that they were free to leave the town, he said that he gave them one local man, and that is not on the record, and I would like that clarified.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters apologise. We did not hear that bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, you may think it useful to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, when you demobilised the men, did you provide them or did you direct them to a local man from Vukovar, and if you did, what was the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Yes. I gave them a man who knew the area well and who could help escort them out of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did they -- did they leave the town as far as you're aware?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Now I know that they did, because they were later captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you stayed in the town because your parents were still there. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So once the men had left, what did you decide to do and where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I went home to be with my parents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you said this was on the 16th that the command had disappeared or had gone. How long did you stay with your parents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: No. I said that in the night between the 16th and the 17th the command ceased to be, and I joined my parents on the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how long did you stay with your parents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: That day and I think the next day as well. Let's say two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what did you decide to do after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Somebody spread the news that people had to gather at the hospital and that some sort of evacuation would take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did you go to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Yes, with my parents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And do you know what date that you arrived at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Well, if my memory serves me right, that would have been the 17th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how long -- how long did you stay at the hospital before you left there?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The witness may have said 19th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, essentially it was one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Is that correct? Did you arrive at the hospital on the 19th, and then you stayed there one day and then you left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: It's not that I left. I was driven away on the 20th in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If we can talk about the day that you arrived at the hospital. Did you place your name on any sort of list at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Yes. My parents recommended me to be put on the list of the wounded, and indeed I had been wounded more than once.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you explain how you were wounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Well, I was wounded in the fighting four times by shrapnel of mines or explosives.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you stayed at the hospital, where did you stay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: For a while I was between the buildings, in the yard, and later I was in the basement, and spent the night on one of the floors of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And during that time that you were at the hospital before you were taken away, did you see any soldiers there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Yes. That day, the 19th, when I arrived in the morning, the army arrived around midday, including one officer on top of an armoured vehicle, and from that point on guards were put in place and entry and exits were restricted. It was all under surveillance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you describe briefly the officer you saw on top of the armoured vehicle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: There was a major in our army, the JNA. The major and the soldiers who were with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court what happened to you the following day when you were taken away from the hospital? How did that day start, and what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Well, it started in the morning around 7.30 or 8.00 a.m. The soldiers who were present were shouting that everybody should leave the premises of the hospital, everybody who could move. I obeyed, and all of us found ourselves outside the hospital where we were searched by the soldiers and directed towards the buses that were to take us away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said the soldiers who were present were shouting. Can you describe the soldiers? You earlier referred to JNA soldiers and paramilitaries attacking the town. Can you give us a sense of who these people about in terms of their grouping?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Well, in my eyes they were all the JNA and people working with the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And these soldiers that were ordering people out, what were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I can't remember now. There was a variety of clothing, but basically all the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you said you were directed towards on the buses -- towards the buses. Did you get on one of those buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Yes. I boarded one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were you the only one on that bus, or did you board with other people from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: No, I wasn't alone. The bus was full.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And who were the people in the bus? Did you know them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: The people on the bus were those who happened to be at the hospital at the time. I knew some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the ones that you knew, were they defenders of the town, or do you know what they did during that two months?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Those that I knew had been involved in the fighting, in the defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And are you able to say the names of those people that were on the same bus as you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Zeljko Jurela; then Damjan Damjanovic, if I'm not mistaken; then a person named Kemal, and his nickname was Kemo. Those are the ones that I'm still sure about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were you told where you were being taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: No. No, they didn't tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And was the bus that you were on guarded at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Yes. There were two men with their light machine-guns trained at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did those men, did they stay on the bus or were they just guarding outside -- outside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: They were on the bus. They never left the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you remember what they were wearing, those men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Well, they looked like men serving -- doing their military service, conscripts wearing uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And about how many buses were out the front of the hospital or in the group that you went towards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I remember three, perhaps four buses standing outside the hospital, but at that time I wasn't particularly paying attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what were you thinking about at that time? What did you think was going to happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I can't remember anymore what I was thinking about, but as we were about to leave town, I thought maybe they would let us reunite with families.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How long were you seated on the bus before they left the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: It didn't take a long time. Ten, 15 minutes, not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And where did you go on that bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
