utterances.text: The buses were facing opposite the road, so first they made a U-turn, and then we headed for the barracks near the fair-grounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe the route that you took on those buses to the fair-grounds? Or near to the fair-grounds, sorry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Right. I can try street by street. First we passed through Gunduliceva Street, then Marko Oreskovic square, Bozidar Adzija Street, Dimitrije Tucovic Street, then Jovan Jovanovic Zmaj Street, Kras Street, and last the fair-grounds all the way up to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you arrived at the barracks, what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: The buses made a half circle on the perimeter of the barracks, and we stood there waiting. I didn't know what we were waiting for.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And at the barracks, about how many buses did you see there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: As I said, three, maybe four, but another two or three came a bit later.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were there any people at the barracks when your bus arrived there and the circle was formed inside it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Yes. The barracks was packed with troops of the JNA. Reservists maybe, or some other forces, I don't know, but it was crawling with troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you put an approximate figure on the number of these troops that were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Several hundred.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And once your bus had parked, what were these troops doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Some of them approached the buses, tried to see if they knew anyone or made threatening signs at individuals. It seemed like a curiosity for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were they saying anything? You said they were using threatening signs. Was anything being said by these troops?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: They did some of that, too, but since we were inside the buses, we couldn't hear all the words. However, some voices carried through the glass, and we could hear some slurs and some threats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you state that they were threatening individuals. Which individuals were they threatening on your bus; do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Specifically, they were threatening Kemo and Damjan Samardzic, as well as Zeljko, Zeljko Jurela. Rade Jakovljevic, also known as Frizider -- Radivoje Jakovljevic, also known as Frizider, was foremost among those making threats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it might be time for the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Smith. We will resume at 20 past 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, before we broke you said that you were seated on the bus and that some of these soldiers were making threats towards some people that you knew on the bus. What were the nature of these threats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: They were death threats. When I look at the transcript, I see Rakovljevic, but he's actually not Rakovljevic, he's Jakovljevic. And his nickname is Hladnjak which translates as "fridge."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And how long were you at the JNA barracks for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: An hour or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Was anyone taken off your bus in that hour or two that you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't think anyone was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what about the other buses? Were you able to see whether anyone was taken off the other buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: It was difficult to see from where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was the atmosphere like outside the buses? You said there was threats being directed to a few people on your bus, but what was the general atmosphere or the mood of these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I'm not sure how I should describe that. There was a lot of commotion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was the mood in the buses? How were you feeling at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I'm not sure how to put it. I felt empty inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Are you able to describe the commotion a bit further that these soldiers had or the atmosphere that seemed to be prevailing around the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't think that I am -- they were probably happy because they had managed to take control of the town, but that's about as much as I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say you were feeling empty, why were you feeling empty at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: We didn't know what would become of us. We knew that we were lost in space and time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were those two guards on the buses that you mentioned earlier, were they giving any indication as to where you were going to go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: No. They weren't telling us anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When the buses left, where did they go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: They left the barracks and turned left in the direction of Negoslavci. They drove us along that road, and some kilometres before Negoslavci they turned off into a field. They took a left turn and came across some sort of a shortcut which they took to take us to Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you were being taken to Ovcara, were you told by anyone where you were going -- where you were going to go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: No, no one told us where we were going. Therefore, we didn't know where we were going.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Whilst you were being taken to Ovcara, what did you think was going to happen to you and the others in the buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I didn't know what was going to happen to us. They were taking us somewhere we didn't know, and we had no idea what would happen to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you explain to the Court Ovcara? Is it a village? What is the location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: It's a farm. There was a pig farm at Ovcara, a good one. People used to live there, but most left at some point, and the only thing remaining there were the farm buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Had you ever been to Ovcara before this day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And about how many times had you been there before, and what would you do in that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I drove by a couple of times. Sometimes I was on my own and sometimes with my parents. I went to that particular area several times for its natural beauty, for its landscape. There was a village nearby called Grabovo with a pond where you could go fishing. I was familiar with the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And about how far in terms of kilometres was Grabovo from Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Not more than five kilometres as the crow flies. The road takes a bit longer than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what happened when you arrived at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: When we arrived, the buses lined up and were emptied. A column was formed which was then sent to an outbuilding there, a hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About how many buses arrived at Ovcara on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: About six.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say a column was formed, who formed this column?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: The column was formed, the buses were emptied, and this was done by the same people who secured the transport, by the people who were on the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say the people that were on the buses, in relation to your particular bus, who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I mean us, the detainees. We were being unloaded from those buses and directed towards that building, the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were the buses unloaded separately or consecutively -- sorry, separately or at the same time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Separately, though one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And do you remember which bus you were in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: The third one, the way I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How long did it take for the buses -- the buses to be unloaded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: About ten minutes, perhaps, or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Was that ten minutes for each bus or ten minutes altogether?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: About ten minutes until I got off.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now when your bus arrived at Ovcara, were there any people there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Yes. There were soldiers standing outside the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you give an indication of the number of the soldiers and the type of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Those were reservists and JNA troops, the mixture of those two. There were probably some paramilitaries there too. Several dozen people. Over 50 possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say that a column was formed between the bus and the outbuilding, the hangar, what happened when that column was formed, if anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: When we arrived outside the door to that hangar, we were stripped of all our valuables and belongings. Our pockets were searched. All our valuables were taken off us, and we were forced to lay all of our belongings down on the ground, including any fur coats or jackets. All valuables and documents were placed on a pile and then people were taken inside the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court as the people in the buses were being formed into a column between the buses and the hangar what the soldiers were doing at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I can't say what everybody was doing, but those soldiers, rather, all those inside the hangar met us in a gauntlet and beat us on the way in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you say you were beaten in a gauntlet, can you describe how you particularly were beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I was struck by an iron bar over the head several times, and I received several blows to my side. I was maybe kicked, or perhaps another implement was used. Perhaps I was punched. It's difficult to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were you hit inside the hangar or outside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you said that, "And the soldiers beat us." Who else did you see being beaten apart from yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Just us, the detainees. I'm not sure who else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About how many other people did you see being beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I don't know how many, but all those who were brought there were made to run the gauntlet. Everybody was beaten and kicked on the way in. After that, people were individually mistreated. That's after all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If we can just talk about the gauntlet for a moment. About how many soldiers were involved in the gauntlet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: It's difficult to say, but I think about 20 on either side, but there was a lot of dust in the air and a general hustle and bustle, so it's difficult to say. At that time, no one was calm enough to count the soldiers. You just ran right through it as fast as you could and were beaten on the way. But I think about 20 people. There may have been 20 people, possibly more.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you said that everybody was beaten and kicked on the way in. Can you tell us where the gauntlet was? Was it inside or outside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, on page 50, line 20, the witness has already said that he was beaten inside the hangar and that the gauntlet itself was inside the hangar. He said so twice, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Carry on, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, was the gauntlet inside or outside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: That's not in dispute. It was inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Once -- once the men on the buses had run through the gauntlet, what happened after that, once the buses were emptied?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Individual mistreatment began. People were beaten and interrogated. The area was closed off. Many people were severely injured. All sorts of implements and tools were used to beat people, rifle-butts, baseball bats, wooden crutches used as an aid by those seriously wounded. The abuse continued inside with varying intensity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you say that the abuse continued inside, was there any abuse outside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I can't say. I was inside. I didn't see what was happening outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: For about how long were you in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: We were there for several hours, until night-time. Until it got dark. Two or three hours perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You've talked about the beatings and the gauntlet when you first came off the buses, and then you talked about the beatings that occurred after that. Which -- which beatings were the most severe?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: The most severe beatings were in those cases where people were beaten to death inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know of anyone that was beaten to death inside the hangar? Do you know their name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Individually, Kemo, Kemal also known as Kemo, was beaten so badly that he died there. He was kicked, stamped on, beaten with rods or, rather, rifle-barrels. I suppose he died there, but I can't be certain. I'm not positive. I can't be positive.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And do you know Kemal's full name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I'm not sure. The nickname was Kemo. I know what he looked like. If you showed me a photograph, I'm sure I'd be able to identify him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that people were beaten to death inside the hangar. Can you tell the Court the other instances that you believe occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I'm not sure if everybody met the same end as Mr. Kemo, but Dado Djukic was another person who was beaten severely with his wooden crutch, the crutch that he used as a walking aid. I'm not sure he could have possibly survived. He was seriously wounded. He had suffered gunshot wounds to both his legs, and he used crutches to walk. He was beaten severely, but I'm not sure how the whole thing ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Are you able to say how many people were inside -- detained inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: It's difficult to say with any degree of certainty, but if one looks at the number of vehicles, and based on what I saw there, there must have been about 300 people detained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And these 300 people, from the ones that you knew are you able to say what ethnic group they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I can't answer that question. One can only assume that most were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Well, that's simple. I never distinguished among people based on their ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And of the -- about how many individuals inside the hangar did you know individually?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I knew quite many of them. I saw a number of them there, and I can tell you who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You can take your time and tell us who they were, and speak slowly so that we can get the name fully recorded on the transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Stanko Duvnjak, a police officer, a member of MUP. Milan Grejza, a MUP inspector. Zeljko Jurela, a defender of Vukovar. Zvonko Varenica, a car mechanic who worked for the hospital's maintenance. Slaven Vukojevic, nicknamed Zambata. Drago Krizan. Vladimir Djukic, nicknamed Dado. Kemo. Oh, I've mentioned him before. I don't know his name, but I knew him before the war. He lived in Vukovar. Damjan Samardzic, another person who was on the bus. That's all I can remember for the time being. If I could have a list, probably I would be able to remember other names and people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I ask that the annex to the indictment be produced to the witness, and if that could be placed on the ELMO starting with the first page and then going consecutively through. Your Honour, I think we have a little problem here at the moment, so we might leave it and come back to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, we'll bring a list to you a bit later so you can have a look at the other names that you saw in the hangar. You said you were in the hangar for at least a couple of hours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in that couple of hours how -- how regular was the beating? Was it constant or was it irregular?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: It happened intermittently. There were breaks, there are lulls, and then the whole thing would take off again with greater force, but it all depends on which individual case we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know why particular people were being beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I can't say why, but it was obviously an act of revenge or something like that. It's difficult to say why people were beaten. But as they were interrogating people, I noticed them focusing more on those who were not from Vukovar, and they seemed even more determined when questioning those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that there were, from your calculations, approximately about 300 people in the hangar. About how many of these people were beaten in the hangar? Can you give an approximate figure or percentage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: It's difficult to say, but everybody was beaten on their way through the gauntlet, but it's difficult to say in relation to each individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that on arrival at the hangar there were JNA soldiers, reserve soldiers, and paramilitaries there. Inside the hangar, can you tell the Court whether any of those soldiers had gone inside the hangar, and if they did, who?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: That's a difficult question. They were all the same to us, those people that we were up against inside. There were probably some White Eagles there. There were some people wearing Chetnik insignia. There was some neat looking people, orderly looking people, proper JNA soldiers. It was a jumble really. There was some locals there from the Vukovar area as well as those who were probably from elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And whilst you were in the hangar, were you questioned by anyone? You said others were questioned, but were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I wasn't questioned myself, but my name was put on a list. The list was compiled by a soldier who went around taking names down. So my personal details were recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what did this soldier look like? How was he dressed? How did he look?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: He was wearing military uniform, camouflage uniform, with a flak jacket on his chest. He looked very soldierly and orderly. He went around and took everybody's names down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that he recorded your personal details. Did he record anything else other than your name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: The date of birth, father's name probably. I don't really remember. All the personal details.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did there appear to be anyone in charge of the soldiers, the reservists, and the paramilitaries that you've stated were inside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Yes. That was the impression. There was a person carrying a whistle, dressed in olive-drab, with a windcheater on. You couldn't tell the rank. This person was using that whistle to orchestrate those people who were there, as it were. That at least was the general impression or, rather, that is how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said this person was wearing a windcheater; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Yes. The military kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Are you able to say how old this person was and the type of build he had, whether he was thin or regular or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: He was of robust build, a bit on the stout side, wearing a moustache and aged about 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Are you able to say what colour his hair was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Dark, perhaps black.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, you said he was using the whistle to orchestrate those people who were there, as it were. What do you mean by that? What was he doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: He was using the whistle to call the soldiers off, those who were mistreating the detainees. They would then calm down, the intensity of the beatings would abate for a while, and then soon enough they'd be back.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: At any one time are you able to say about how many soldiers were involved in the beatings inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: It's difficult to judge. About 50, perhaps, about a hundred. I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when these detainees were being beaten, what were the rest of the detainees doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Everybody was just somewhere, and there was nothing for any of us to do. We just waited to see what would happen next.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were the detainees, were they standing? Were they seated? Were they on the ground? Can you explain how they were in these one or two hours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Some were standing. Some were lying down on the ground. Most of them were seated, and some were being moved by those people from one spot to another, changing their positions, as it were, inside the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Apart from the detainees that were placed in the hangar and the soldiers, was there anything else in the building, any machinery, any -- anything other than those people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: There was only hay in the part of the building where we were. In the front part of the building there was a desk, the kind you usually see in schools, just a regular desk, and there was a length of rope attached to it, and there were some detainees behind that. There was another section of the building that we didn't go to, it's quite a long hall, and there was some sort of a vehicle there, a piece of machinery, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was the atmosphere like for you when the beatings were continuing in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: It was dreadful. We were just waiting, feeling an enormous fear and feeling that an evil would strike us. It's difficult to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when the beatings were continuing against the detainees, were the other detainees trying to stop the beatings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: No. They couldn't even budge, let alone speak up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the -- the soldier with the whistle, did he say anything to the detainees during that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I didn't notice him saying anything to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: At any stage were any of the detainees taken outside of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Some were taken outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you explain how that happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Two soldiers would come, approach a person and say, "You're coming with us." I can't give you any more details. I saw them take out Sinisa Glavasevic and one young man from the defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were detainees taken out individually or in groups? Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Individually.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court how you left the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: After that time that I cannot define that I spent there, they started taking out people in groups, in an organised way. The groups would include ten or 20 people. They were lined up and taken out the same door through which they had been brought in. And that went on until I was taken out myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When the first group was taken out, are you able to say whether it was light or dark outside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: It was getting dark while we were still inside, and the lights were on. Probably a power unit and a generator were working outside for the lights inside to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And about how many groups were taken out before you were taken out of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Two groups, I think. I think I was in the third one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court who took your group out and what happened once you got outside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: We were brought out by soldiers or, rather, soldier, the same soldier who took out the first and the second group. I think it was the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was this soldier wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: He was a regular soldier, with epaulettes of a regular soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the colour of the uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Olive-grey, the colour of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did this soldier say anything to you when he took you out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: He told us that we were going to be transferred to another hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, I believe, has something to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Vasic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. On page 60, line 2, I think the witness was talking about an ordinary soldier and the translation says "regular soldier." I'm not sure that's correct. An ordinary soldier does not necessarily belong to regular units. Could the -- could the -- my colleague clarify it with the witness perhaps? I think the translation, the interpretation, is not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, was he an ordinary soldier or a regular soldier? How would you put it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Do you think I was in a position to ask him whether he was ordinary or extraordinary? He was a soldier of the JNA and that was enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And once you left the hangar, where did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: We were put in a military vehicle, a JNA vehicle, and transferred towards Grabovo. Almost halfway, in a depression the vehicle braked, lowered its speed, turned left and turned towards the swamp that was part of that farm between Ovcara and Grabovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Perhaps before we discuss what happened at this point, can you give us an understanding of the time that passed from the time that the first group was taken out until you left the hangar? Approximately how long was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I think it was ten to 15 minutes, the time that it took for one group by another to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you describe the military truck that you were placed on, or the military vehicle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: It was a regular ordinary vehicle, freight vehicle of the JNA, capacity two tonnes, maybe, covered with a tarpaulin. Nothing special, apart from the fact that it was military vehicle, an army vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And apart from your group that got on the truck, did that soldier that came to get you from the hangar, did he also travel with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: No. He had joined the driver, and there was practically nobody with us in the back of that vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was the lighting like outside at this time? Was it light or dark? Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I've already said that it was getting dark while we were still inside the hangar, but there was moonlight. Although it was dark outside there was moonlight, so there was some visibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did you know any of the other people in your group that were placed in the truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Yes, I knew some.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what were their names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Zeljko Jurela was one. And one man from Sotin. His name eludes me right now, but I'll remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you know a Mato Perak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's the person. Mato Perak from Sotin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And as you were travelling out in this military truck, was there any discussions between either yourself and Zeljko, Mato, and any of the other detainees placed in the truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Not much, but when Mato, who was trying to peer through the tarpaulin and wanted to get out, Zeljko stopped him by saying, "Don't. They'll kill us all." He was trying to dissuade him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that the soldier that took you out of the hangar said you were being taken to another hangar. Whilst you were in the military truck, did you believe that to be the case, that you were going to another hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Well, partly I did believe that because I knew there were other hangars in Grabovo, but I wasn't sure there were some in this area. In the army, it's possible to make some sort of makeshift accommodation using tents, even in a clearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What did you decide to do as the truck was travelling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I decided to jump. I gripped something above me and jumped, and then I looked back to see if anyone would follow, if anyone would do the same, or if the vehicle would stop. That was another possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And why did you decide to jump?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: It's a moment I cannot describe, because I was in a state of shock after all the beating and everything that had happened, all the bad things that we had been through. It was just an instantaneous decision. I did what I did. I jumped.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And after you jumped, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I set out in the direction of Vukovar, passing by the pig farm, heading for Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And as you set out in that direction, did you hear anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Yes. I heard several shots. There was the sound of the vehicle stopping, braking. The noise of the vehicle subsided. I heard a short volley of fire and several individual shots from the direction from which I was going.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About how long after you jumped off the truck did you hear this shooting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: A minute, two.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you see the truck when the shooting was occurring?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: No. No, I couldn't see it anymore. It was still night. It was still dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And after you heard that, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I tried to keep the direction I had decided on, heading for Vukovar. And before a place called Ljutik, I passed through a cornfield and by the fair-grounds and continued in the vicinity of Bogdanovci village heading for Vinkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And where did you go after what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: As I said before, I was heading for Vinkovci, which I thought was still under the control of our forces, and I was trying to get to the free territory of the Republic of Croatia. My aim was to join my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were you able to get to the free territory or not, and if you didn't, where did you end up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I ended up a prisoner, because passing through Ceric village, I turned back. And after several hours of hard walking and trying to get out of there, I was exhausted and thirsty. I tried to find some water somewhere, and since it was already dawning, I thought I would get water somewhere, and I thought there were maybe some civilians in the basement that was quite close in front of me, or maybe that it was empty. However, what I did was I woke up some reservists of the JNA instead, and that's when I was taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you intentionally wake them up or was that by accident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: By accident. I was going there to get some water. I asked in a loud voice, "Is there anyone there?" Hoping that there would be ordinary people there, not the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you said that you were taken prisoner. What happened when that happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: They put me in a smoking house from which I tried to escape several times, but the third time I attempted an escape a soldier who stood guard there fired from his automatic rifle, told me, "If you try this once again, I'll shoot straight through you."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how long were you kept prisoner there after you tried to escape for the third time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: That night was a short one, because it was practically sunrise when I got there, and it was day just an hour or two after I got there. And then they took me to some sort of command post they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you describe the command post, who was there? Were there any soldiers present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: There were soldiers outside that command post, which was in fact an ordinary house converted into a command post, and there were soldiers there. They interrogated me, threatened me, beat me, and they took some things from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You say they interrogated you. What were they asking you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: What I had been doing, where I had been. I can't remember all the things they asked me anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you said they beat you. How severely did they beat you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Right. They beat me severely enough so that I started bleeding from my head, and then the beating stopped shortly afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how long was the beating for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Not long. Five to ten minutes. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how long did you stay at this headquarters for before you were taken somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Well, for a very short while, maybe 15 minutes before they put me on a truck, an army truck. And I had a soldier for an escort. He kept his automatic rifle or light machine-gun trained at me all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what type of soldier was he? You talked about paramilitaries, reserves, regular soldiers. Can you describe what group he belonged to or what he wore?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: He wore military clothing, but I told you before that I couldn't tell by the clothes who belonged to which group, but it was a JNA uniform. I don't know whether he was a regular or paramilitary. At that time, there was no pattern. He was a soldier in any case, either a regular soldier or mobilised as a reservist.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And where were you taken and what happened to you at this place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: They took me to a place calmed Stari Jankovci, and there I was handed over to the military police. I believe there was a captain there who questioned me. And after that, he sent me to the basement where two policemen beat me up. And there were some other prisoners down there who had been brought earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how did you know they were the military police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Well, in the JNA, they were recognisable by white belts worn like suspenders. So they had this olive-grey uniform with white suspender belts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you describe the beating that you received at -- at this place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: They beat us with truncheons, those other men, and me in particular. The beating was done by truncheons until the victim would fall to the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did they say anything to you, the military police, before they beat you up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I don't remember them saying anything. Maybe they did, maybe they didn't. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did you receive any injuries from this beating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: No particular injuries, but I was all black and blue all over my body.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said you were taken to a basement and that's where you were beaten. What type of premises was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: It was a house converted into some sort of accommodation for JNA troops, maybe like a command post for the military police or headquarters. Otherwise, it was a normal farmhouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were you questioned at all by anyone whilst you were in the basement of this house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Not in the basement, but in the ground floor of the house. That's where I was questioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And who questioned you, can you describe him, and also, what was the question about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Well, it was an officer who questioned me. I think he was a captain by rank, a JNA captain. And the questions had to do with my role in the defence of the town, the laying of mines in minefields, where I put, how many mines, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how do you know he was a JNA captain?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: He wore the signs of his rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: After the questioning, what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: After the questioning, he handcuffed me to the radiator and that's where I spent the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the next morning did you go anywhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: The next morning those of us who were kept there were all put in a van and transported to Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how many others of you were kept there, and do you know what they had done to end up at that place as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: I don't know. They used to live in Vukovar, and what they had or hadn't done I don't know. In any case, they were prisoners, three of them, or maybe even four. One was even a member from Dzakova, and several of us were taken to Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What sort of vehicle took you to Sid, and who was driving it, and what happened when you got there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: It was an ordinary vehicle, not an army one. It's like a Volkswagen van. And we were driven to the police station in Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how long did you stay at the police station there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Several hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were you questioned at the police station, and if you were, what about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Yes. We were questioned about what had been going on there, who had been where.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say "what had been going on there," are you referring to Vukovar generally or anything in particular?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: It was questioning in general terms, but my particular interrogator asked me how many people had been killed at Ovcara, because he seemed to remember me from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The person that was doing the interrogating, was he a police officer, someone in the army, or from some other group, or a civilian?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: He was dressed in civilian clothes. I suppose he was an inspector, maybe of the MUP. That means civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How long did the discussion continue for in relation to how many people had been killed at Ovcara? How long did that discussion go on for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: It was very brief, because I denied knowing him at all, and that was the end of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And why did you think that he seemed to remember you from being at Ovcara? Why did you think that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: That's not what I thought. He claimed that he remembered me from Ovcara, and he wanted to know -- he wanted me to tell me -- to tell him how many people had been there and had been killed there, and I couldn't tell him that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did he tell you what he was doing at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: No. The only thing that he said was that the two of us had seen each other at Ovcara, which led me to believe that he must have been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that you were at the police station for a couple of hours. After that -- after that time there, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Again, some JNA soldiers came to fetch us, and as we were leaving the cell, they beat us first and then threw us into a truck, a JNA truck, and covered in blood and beaten up as we were, we were driven to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And where were you taken to at Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Well, we were taken to the civilian prison of Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in this prison?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011
utterances.text: Until the 4th of February, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And whilst you were at the prison, were you interviewed at all in relation to your involvement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, I'm judging that your next question will lead to several, and I'm looking at the time and the tape. I think we have to call it an evening at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: There's no objection from the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will, therefore, adjourn at this stage and resume again tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
